Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
go along with whatever others want to feel safe

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Arjun is a 41-year-old South Asian man who works as a park ranger in a mid-Atlantic national forest, a role he sought out, he once explained to his intake clinician, precisely because it kept him away from crowds and uniforms. He has been in a relationship for three years, though his partner has recently begun expressing concern about the emotional distance that has grown between them. Arjun presented for treatment after a routine park service briefing - attended by several officers from a neighbouring jurisdiction, all in uniform - left him unable to drive home and sitting in his truck for two hours, unable to account for the time.

Approximately four years ago, Arjun was taken captive during a hiking trip abroad. He was held for eleven days by a small armed group whose members wore military-style fatigues and conducted themselves with the rigid, performative authority of soldiers. During that time he was restrained, deprived of food as a method of control, and subjected to sustained humiliation - made to speak on command, to stand and sit on order, to demonstrate submission in front of multiple captors simultaneously. He was watched constantly. The experience of being seen, scrutinised, and assessed for compliance became as threatening as the physical deprivation itself. When he was eventually released, he was physically weakened and, as he would later describe it, "completely emptied out."

In the months that followed, Arjun found that certain moments fractured without warning into what he calls "photographs" - discrete, frozen images from the captivity, each carrying a precise sensory weight. One image is of a captor's boots at eye level. Another is of his own hands, bound. When these fragments surface, he sometimes feels a dull, spreading ache across his wrists and lower back - the body replaying what the mind cannot fully integrate. On other occasions the same memories arrive entirely stripped of feeling, as though he is reading a report about someone else. These memory intrusions are reliably activated by specific cues: conversations about military topics, the sight of a person in uniform, or the simple, ordinary experience of being looked at. A hiker pausing to ask him for directions can be enough - the sense of being seen triggers the image-sequence, and the images in turn confirm what he has come to believe about himself: that he is permanently marked by what happened, that he was uniquely foolish to have been placed in that situation, that another man - a stronger, more vigilant man - would never have been captured at all.

This appraisal of permanent humiliation and personal deficiency has not remained static. It has actively shaped how Arjun moves through his days, and in doing so it has kept the wound open. He goes along with whatever colleagues or his partner suggest, unable to assert a preference or decline a request, because compliance feels like the safest posture available - a logic that was installed during eleven days in which compliance was survival. But people-pleasing returns him, in quieter moments, to the memory of performing submission for armed men, and the self-disgust that follows re-activates the very sense of humiliation it was meant to forestall. He also controls his eating with considerable rigidity - scheduling meals, measuring portions, refusing spontaneity around food - because this is the one domain in which deprivation cannot be imposed on him again. Yet the hypervigilance required to maintain that control keeps his nervous system in a state of low-grade alert, and that alert state makes the intrusive images more accessible, not less. He has entertained detailed revenge fantasies about the men who held him, and while these briefly restore a sense of agency, they also require him to mentally re-enter the captivity, sharpening the memory's edges and intensifying the physical pain that accompanies recall.

The threat-monitoring that now governs his daily life is most visible at work. Unexpected movement - a deer breaking from undergrowth, a colleague stepping around a corner - produces a full-body startle that he cannot modulate. He cannot accept reassurance that he is safe; when his partner tells him he is home, he knows it intellectually and disbelieves it entirely. These moments of hyperarousal feed back into the memory, making each recollection feel more recent and more dangerous, and each cycle of threat and recall deepens his conviction that he is irreparably changed. He feels isolated in a way that has become structural - not merely lonely, but separated from other people by an experience he cannot translate.

What finally brought him in was not the two hours in the truck, though that frightened him. It was his partner saying, quietly, that they felt they were living with someone who was still somewhere else. Arjun wants, more than anything, to stop being watched by his own memory.
